skill.title: Linux
skill.summary: Working on Linux servers: processes, signals, files, permissions and the shell.
skill.description: Inspect and control processes and services. Reason about files, permissions and ownership. Compose shell commands and scripts that fail safely.

questions.title: Reading a permission string
questions.prompt: `ls -l` shows `-rwxr-x---` for `deploy.sh`. Which `chmod` mode produces exactly these permissions?
questions.hint: Read, write and execute are worth 4, 2 and 1.

options.text: `chmod 755 deploy.sh`
`chmod 750 deploy.sh`
`chmod 640 deploy.sh`
`chmod 570 deploy.sh`

questions.explanation: Each group of three bits is read (4), write (2) and execute (1). The owner has `rwx` = 7, the group has `r-x` = 5, and others have `---` = 0, giving 750. 755 would also let everyone else read and execute the script.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “chmod 750 deploy.sh”. Each group of three bits is read (4), write (2) and execute (1).
rubric: Converts each triplet to a digit.
Assigns owner, group and others in that order.
Arrives at 750.
misconceptions: The digits are ordered others, group, owner.
Execute is worth 4.

questions.title: What plain kill sends
questions.prompt: You run `kill 4321` with no options. What happens?
questions.hint: Which signal number does `kill` use by default?

options.text: The kernel immediately terminates the process; it cannot react
The process receives `SIGTERM` and may clean up before exiting
The process is paused until you resume it with `SIGCONT`
The process is restarted by the kernel with the same PID

questions.explanation: Without an option, `kill` sends `SIGTERM` (signal 15). A process can catch it to finish requests, flush files and exit cleanly, or ignore it. `SIGKILL` (9) is the signal that cannot be caught or ignored; use it only when a process will not stop otherwise, because it gets no chance to clean up.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “The process receives `SIGTERM` and may clean up before exiting”. Without an option, `kill` sends `SIGTERM` (signal 15).
rubric: Identifies SIGTERM as the default.
Explains that SIGTERM can be handled.
Contrasts it with SIGKILL, which cannot be caught.
misconceptions: `kill` always forcibly kills.
Any signal can be caught.

questions.title: One character that erased a log
questions.prompt: `app.log` holds a week of logs. You meant to add one line to it but ran `echo "restarted" > app.log`. What is in the file now?
questions.hint: What does the shell do to the file before `echo` runs?

options.text: The week of logs followed by `restarted`
Only the line `restarted`
Nothing; the shell refuses to overwrite a file
The week of logs; `echo` cannot write to files

questions.explanation: `>` opens the file for writing and truncates it to zero length before the command runs, so the old content is gone and only `restarted` remains. `>>` appends instead. Bash's `set -o noclobber` makes `>` refuse to overwrite an existing file, but it is off by default.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “Only the line `restarted”. `>` opens the file for writing and truncates it to zero length before the command runs, so the old content is gone and only `restarted` remains.
rubric: Explains that `>` truncates the file.
Names `>>` for appending.
Mentions noclobber as an optional safeguard.
misconceptions: `>` appends to existing files.
The shell warns before overwriting by default.

questions.title: Readable file, permission denied
questions.prompt: `/srv/app/config.yml` has mode `644`, but its directory `/srv/app` has mode `700` and is owned by `appuser`. A different user runs `cat /srv/app/config.yml`. What happens and why?
questions.hint: What permission does a process need on `/srv/app` to look up a name inside it?

options.text: It works, because the file itself is world-readable
Permission denied, because the directory lacks execute (search) permission for others
Permission denied, because the file lacks execute permission for others
It works, but only if the user already knows the exact path

questions.explanation: To reach a file, a process needs execute (search) permission on every directory in its path. With `700`, users other than the owner (and root) cannot traverse `/srv/app`, so opening the file fails before its own mode is checked. Directory read permission is for listing names; execute is for using them. A file's execute bit is irrelevant to reading it.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “Permission denied, because the directory lacks execute (search) permission for others”. To reach a file, a process needs execute (search) permission on every directory in its path.
rubric: Explains path traversal needs execute on each directory.
Distinguishes directory read (list) from execute (traverse).
Notes the file's own mode is never reached.
misconceptions: A world-readable file is readable whatever its directory.
Reading a file needs its execute bit.

questions.title: A process that kill -9 cannot remove
questions.prompt: `ps` shows dozens of processes in state `Z` (`<defunct>`) under one parent service. `kill -9` on them has no effect. What is going on?
questions.hint: Is a zombie process still running code?

options.text: They are hung in disk I/O and will exit when the disk responds
They have exited, but the parent has not called `wait` to collect their status
They are protected kernel threads that ignore all signals
They are stopped processes waiting for `SIGCONT`

questions.explanation: A zombie is a child that has already exited; the kernel keeps a small process-table entry holding its exit status until the parent reaps it with `wait`/`waitpid`. There is nothing left to kill. Fix the parent so it reaps children (or handles `SIGCHLD`); if the parent exits, `init` adopts and reaps the zombies. Large numbers can exhaust PIDs.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “They have exited, but the parent has not called `wait` to collect their status”. A zombie is a child that has already exited; the kernel keeps a small process-table entry holding its exit status until the parent reaps it with `wait`/`waitpid`.
rubric: Explains that zombies have already exited.
Explains that the parent must reap them with wait.
Explains why signals do nothing.
Proposes fixing or restarting the parent.
misconceptions: Zombies use CPU and memory like running processes.
`kill -9` removes any process.

questions.title: A backup script that uploaded nothing
questions.prompt: A nightly script starts with `set -e` and runs `pg_dump shop | gzip > shop.sql.gz`, then uploads the file. One night `pg_dump` fails with an authentication error, yet the script carries on and uploads a tiny, useless backup. Why?
questions.hint: Which command's exit status does a pipeline report, and what does gzip do with empty input?

options.text: `set -e` is ignored for commands whose output is redirected to a file
A pipeline's status is that of its last command unless `pipefail` is set
`pg_dump` exits with status 0 even when authentication fails
`set -e` only applies to commands that run inside a function

questions.explanation: By default a pipeline returns the exit status of its last command. `pg_dump` fails, but `gzip` happily compresses the empty stream and exits 0, so the pipeline counts as a success and `set -e` never triggers. `set -o pipefail` makes the pipeline fail if any command in it fails. Also verify the artefact before uploading it, for example with a minimum size or a test restore.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “A pipeline's status is that of its last command unless `pipefail` is set”. By default a pipeline returns the exit status of its last command.
rubric: Explains that a pipeline's status comes from its last command.
Explains that gzip succeeds on empty input.
Proposes `set -o pipefail`.
Suggests verifying the backup before upload.
misconceptions: `set -e` catches failures anywhere in a pipeline.
A file that exists is a valid backup.

questions.title: A full disk that du cannot explain
questions.prompt: `df -h /` reports the root filesystem 100% full, but `du -sh /` accounts for only half of it. Last night someone ran `rm` on a 40 GB log file that a running service writes to. What explains the gap, and what frees the space?
questions.hint: When are a deleted file's blocks actually released?

options.text: The filesystem's journal still holds the file; run `fsck` to clear it
The file's blocks stay allocated while a process holds it open; restart or reopen the log
`du` cannot see files over 4 GB; use `ls -la` to find the space
Deleted files move to a hidden trash directory; empty it to free space

questions.explanation: `rm` removes the directory entry (unlink), but the inode and its blocks are freed only when the last open file descriptor closes. The service still holds the file, so `df` counts the space while `du`, which walks names, cannot see it. Find it with `lsof +L1` (or `ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd`), then restart the service or make it reopen its logs; in an emergency, truncate through `/proc/<pid>/fd/<n>`. Use log rotation that signals the service instead of deleting live files.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “The file's blocks stay allocated while a process holds it open; restart or reopen the log”. `rm` removes the directory entry (unlink), but the inode and its blocks are freed only when the last open file descriptor closes.
rubric: Explains unlink removes the name but not the open inode.
Explains why df and du disagree.
Finds the file with lsof or /proc.
Frees space by restarting, reopening or truncating.
misconceptions: Deleting a file always frees its space immediately.
df and du should always agree.

questions.title: Exit code 137 under load
questions.prompt: A worker process dies during a large batch with exit status 137 and nothing in its own logs. `dmesg` contains `Out of memory: Killed process ... (worker)`. What happened?
questions.hint: Exit statuses above 128 encode a signal number.

options.text: The worker caught `SIGTERM` and chose to exit with status 137
The kernel's OOM killer sent `SIGKILL` (128 + 9 = 137) when memory ran out
The worker hit a segmentation fault, which always maps to status 137
The filesystem filled up and the kernel stopped the process with `SIGSTOP`

questions.explanation: Shells report a process killed by signal N as 128 + N; 137 is 128 + 9, `SIGKILL`. When the system or a cgroup runs out of memory, the kernel's OOM killer picks a victim and sends it `SIGKILL`, which cannot be caught, so the process logs nothing. Confirm with `dmesg` or `journalctl -k`, then reduce memory use (stream the batch, cap batch size), raise the memory limit, or adjust `oom_score_adj` deliberately.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “The kernel's OOM killer sent `SIGKILL` (128 + 9 = 137) when memory ran out”. Shells report a process killed by signal N as 128 + N; 137 is 128 + 9, `SIGKILL`.
rubric: Decodes 137 as 128 + SIGKILL.
Attributes it to the OOM killer using the kernel log.
Explains why the process logs nothing.
Proposes reducing memory use or adjusting limits.
misconceptions: Exit 137 means the program has a bug that returned 137.
The application can always log before being killed.

questions.title: A cleanup script with an empty variable
questions.prompt: A cleanup script runs `rm -rf $BUILD_DIR/*`. One night `BUILD_DIR` is not set. What does the shell run, and what is the most robust guard?
questions.hint: What does `$BUILD_DIR/*` become when the variable is empty?

options.text: `rm -rf /*`; use `rm -rf "${BUILD_DIR:?}"/*` (and `set -u`) so an unset or empty variable aborts the script
Nothing; Bash refuses to run a command when one of its variables is unset, so no guard is needed
`rm -rf *` in the current directory; wrap the whole command in an `if [ -d "$BUILD_DIR" ]` check
`rm -rf /*`, but GNU `rm` defaults to `--preserve-root`, which blocks it, so no guard is needed

questions.explanation: An unset variable expands to nothing, so the command becomes `rm -rf /*`. `--preserve-root` (the GNU default) only refuses the literal `/`, not the expanded list `/bin /etc ...`, so it does not help. `${BUILD_DIR:?}` makes the shell exit with an error if the variable is unset or empty; `set -u` catches unset variables generally; quoting prevents word splitting if the path contains spaces.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “rm -rf /*`; use `rm -rf "${BUILD_DIR:?}"/*` (and `set -u`) so an unset or empty variable aborts the script”. An unset variable expands to nothing, so the command becomes `rm -rf /*`.
rubric: Shows the expansion to `rm -rf /*`.
Explains why --preserve-root does not protect against `/*`.
Uses `${VAR:?}` and/or `set -u`.
Quotes the expansion.
misconceptions: Unset variables make Bash skip the command.
--preserve-root protects against all root deletions.

questions.title: High load average, idle CPUs
questions.prompt: A 4-core server shows a load average of 40, yet `top` reports the CPUs about 85% idle and requests are timing out. Explain what Linux load average measures and walk through how you would diagnose this.
questions.hint: Which process states does Linux include in the load average?
questions.explanation: On Linux, load average counts tasks that are runnable *and* tasks in uninterruptible sleep (state D), which is usually waiting on disk or network I/O such as NFS. High load with idle CPUs therefore points at blocked I/O, not CPU saturation. Check `top`/`vmstat 1` for high `wa` (iowait) and the `b` column, `ps -eo state,pid,cmd | grep '^D'` to see which processes are blocked and on what (`/proc/<pid>/stack`, `wchan`), `iostat -x 1` for device utilisation and await times, `dmesg` for disk or NFS errors, and memory pressure (`free`, swap activity in `vmstat`, PSI in `/proc/pressure/io`). Fix the cause: a failing or saturated disk, a hung network mount, swap thrashing, or an application issuing too much synchronous I/O, and add alerting on I/O latency rather than load alone.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Explains that Linux load includes uninterruptible (D-state) tasks, infers I/O blocking, and uses iowait, D-state process listing, iostat and kernel logs to find the device or mount responsible.
rubric: Explains that Linux load counts runnable and D-state tasks.
Infers I/O blocking from high load with idle CPU.
Uses vmstat/top iowait and lists D-state processes.
Checks device latency with iostat and errors in dmesg.
Considers memory pressure and swap, and proposes better alerting.
misconceptions: Load average is CPU utilisation.
A load above the core count always means the CPUs are saturated.
